clinicalPearls: Deposition of basic calcium phosphate (mainly hydroxyapatite) crystals in periarticular and articular tissues
Calcific tendinitis, especially of the rotator cuff, is a common manifestation causing acute severe shoulder pain
In the shoulder it can cause the destructive Milwaukee shoulder syndrome with a large effusion and cuff arthropathy
The crystals are too small to see with ordinary light microscopy and are not birefringent, unlike urate and CPP crystals
Alizarin red staining or advanced techniques are needed to identify the crystals
Radiographs show amorphous periarticular calcification; treatment is largely symptomatic with some cases needing aspiration or barbotage
reference.pathophysiology: Basic calcium phosphate deposition disease involves the accumulation of hydroxyapatite and related crystals in tendons, bursae and joints. In tendons this causes calcific tendinitis, and crystal shedding provokes acute inflammation. Within joints, particularly the shoulder, the crystals stimulate release of enzymes that degrade cartilage and cause a rapidly destructive arthropathy (Milwaukee shoulder). The very small, non-birefringent crystals are difficult to detect, so the diagnosis is often made on the clinical and radiographic picture.
additionalInvestigations: Synovial fluid analysis (crystals not seen on standard microscopy; alizarin red where available)
Exclusion of infection when acutely inflamed
Assessment of joint destruction in suspected Milwaukee shoulder
redFlags: Features suggesting septic arthritis or bursitis
reference.prognosis: Calcific tendinitis is often self-limiting and responds to conservative measures or barbotage, whereas destructive BCP arthropathy of the shoulder has a poorer functional prognosis.
pitfalls: Failing to detect the crystals because they are invisible on standard microscopy
Confusing it with CPPD or gout
Missing septic arthritis in an acutely inflamed joint
Underestimating the destructive potential in the shoulder
management: Manage acute calcific tendinitis symptomatically with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, with colchicine or a short corticosteroid course for severe flares
Perform ultrasound-guided barbotage (needle aspiration and lavage) of hydroxyapatite deposits for persistent rotator-cuff calcific tendinitis
Offer image-guided peri-tendinous corticosteroid injection when conservative measures fail, after excluding infection by aspiration and culture
Provide physiotherapy and graded shoulder rehabilitation to restore movement and function
Consider extracorporeal shock-wave therapy or arthroscopic removal for large refractory deposits
In destructive Milwaukee shoulder, use analgesia, aspiration of large effusions and physiotherapy, with shoulder arthroplasty for advanced joint destruction
Refer to rheumatology or orthopaedics for resistant or destructive disease
